clue.text: Bird seed has sex appeal

parts.note: a pip is the small seed of an apple or orange
IT is old slang for sex appeal, as in the 'It girl'

explanation.surface: A packet of birdseed is somehow alluring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird seed' reads as food for a budgie, but 'Bird' is the definition and 'seed' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The pipit is a small brown songbird of fields and moorland.

clue.text: Show father some support when 'e's inside

parts.note: pa is father

indicators.note: inside tells us the letter goes within the supporting frame

parts.note: a gantry is a supporting frame, as for cranes or signals
'e is he with the h dropped, leaving just E

explanation.surface: A dad gives a bit of support when his son is at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts E within GANTRY. The 's of ''e's' means 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Pageantry is splendid display and ceremonial spectacle.

clue.text: Greyish sort of green on both sides

parts.note: pea green is a shade of green
both sides are right and left, R and L

explanation.surface: A dull green colour appears on either side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'both sides' gives R and L, right and left.
explanation.definitionFit: Pearl grey is a pale bluish-grey, the colour of a pearl.

clue.text: Elegant set out of order — external fault, perhaps?

indicators.note: external says one group of letters goes around the outside of the other
perhaps says the word is only one possible arrangement of its letters
out of order tells us to jumble the letters of the word before

explanation.surface: Something smart is broken, perhaps an outside defect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'external' puts one rearranged word around the other: TAFUL outside STE. 'fault, perhaps' looks like a tennis serve gone wrong, but 'perhaps' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasteful means showing good judgement in style, refined.

clue.text: Boy and helper falling out — that's an exaggeration

indicators.note: falling out suggests a quarrel that throws the letters of these two words into disorder

explanation.surface: A boy and his helper quarrel, and someone overstates the row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falling out' looks like a quarrel between the boy and his helper, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyperbole is the figure of speech that overstates for effect.

clue.text: Bear up 16

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh is the famous bear of A A Milne's stories

explanation.surface: A bear rises up.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 is RING, from 16 across. 'Bear' looks like a verb, but it is Pooh the bear, read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoop is a circular band, so a ring.

clue.text: Before vicar comes in, how-should he behave?

indicators.note: comes in says the title goes into the adverb

parts.note: a vicar ought to behave piously, devoutly
Rev, the Reverend, is the title of a vicar

explanation.surface: Before the vicar enters, people wonder how he ought to conduct himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The question is answered by PIOUSLY, and REV 'comes in' to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Previously means earlier, at a prior time.

clue.text: For a pleasurable walk, it's right to go at an easy pace

parts.note: to amble is to walk slowly and easily

explanation.surface: A walker says it is proper to stroll at leisure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' and 'it's' and 'to' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A ramble is a leisurely country walk taken for enjoyment.

clue.text: A contrary argument I take on purpose first

indicators.note: first says the purpose comes before the other pieces

parts.note: an object is an aim or purpose

explanation.surface: Someone deliberately takes the opposing line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on purpose' looks like 'deliberately', but 'on' and 'purpose' do separate jobs; 'first' brings the purpose ahead of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: An objection is a reason given against something, an opposing case.

clue.text: Join up — the king's in solitary confinement!

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the whole is read from the bottom
in places the king inside the solitary word

parts.note: lone means solitary
R stands for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone joins up, while the king is locked away alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Join up' looks like the definition, but 'up' reverses LORNE (R in LONE).
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to sign up as a member.

clue.text: Politician pleased at putting on ' weight

parts.note: glad means pleased
a stone is a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A politician is happy to have put on a few pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting on' reads as gaining weight; here it just sets one piece beside the other. GLADSTONE was a Victorian British prime minister; a STONE is fourteen pounds, still used in Britain for body weight.
explanation.definitionFit: William Gladstone served four times as Liberal prime minister in Victorian Britain.

clue.text: He wears a crown of greater size

explanation.walkthrough: 'He wears a crown' suggests a king, but it is the army officer whose insignia is a crown.
explanation.definitionFit: A British army major's rank badge is a crown on the shoulder; major also means larger or more important.

clue.text: Like the jump of a salmon, say, or like a kipper?

indicators.note: say signals that the words before are heard rather than spelt

parts.words: Like the jump of a salmon
parts.note: as means like; a salmon's jump upstream is called a leap

explanation.surface: A leaping salmon is compared with a smoked fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kipper' looks like the smoked herring to go with the salmon, but here it is someone having a kip (British slang for a sleep).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone kipping is sleeping, so they are dozing and not awake.

clue.text: The foundation of Babylon, 11B.C., all written about in scripture

indicators.note: the foundation of a word is where it starts, so take only its opening letter
written about suggests the letters are written in a different arrangement

parts.note: 11 reads as the Roman numeral II, two ones, and B.C. gives BC

explanation.surface: Ancient Babylon's founding date is recorded in holy writ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'written about' rearranges B (the first letter of Babylon), II, BC and ALL. The date looks historical, but the digits stand for two letter I's.
explanation.definitionFit: Biblical describes what comes from or appears in the Bible, the Christian holy writings.

clue.text: A real bitch strangely generous

indicators.note: strangely says the letters of these words are oddly arranged

explanation.surface: A nasty woman behaves with surprising kindness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' rearranges A, REAL and BITCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Charitable means kind and giving to others.

clue.text: During all, or most of the sketch

indicators.note: most of means the word that follows loses its final letter

parts.note: to rough out a plan is to sketch it

explanation.surface: Something lasts for the whole show, or nearly all of the comic sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' trims THE to TH. 'sketch' looks like a comedy item, but it is the verb ROUGH OUT, to draft roughly.
explanation.definitionFit: Throughout means from start to finish, for the whole of a period.

clue.text: Managed business, or put up with us showing spite

parts.note: ran means managed
Co is short for company, a business

indicators.note: put up in a down clue says the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A firm's owners are spiteful to us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up with' looks like 'tolerate', but 'put up' turns OR into RO.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancorous means bitter and resentful.

clue.text: Call round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Call round' reads as a visit to someone's house; split it into two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring is to telephone, and a ring is a circle.

clue.text: Construction lacking any firm foundation

parts.note: construction is an interpretation put on facts, here one built without evidence, not a building

explanation.walkthrough: 'Construction' looks like a building with no footings; it means an interpretation.
explanation.definitionFit: A guess is a theory built without solid evidence, the way a building without footings has nothing firm beneath it.

clue.text: Issue notes in duplicate with this pen

indicators.note: in duplicate says the word appears twice

parts.note: to sing is to issue musical notes

explanation.surface: A prison clerk issues notes in duplicate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pen' looks like a writing pen, but it is a prison: SING SING is a prison in New York State.
explanation.definitionFit: Sing Sing is a famous prison, and a pen is short for penitentiary.

clue.text: Foreigner with some pull

explanation.walkthrough: 'with some' just links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Yank is British slang for an American, a foreigner here, and a yank is a sharp tug.

clue.text: For splendour, I'll take Haver-gal round to church

indicators.note: take round says the name goes around the other letters
take round says the name goes around the other letters

parts.note: Havergal Brian was an English composer, so his first name leads to his surname
the apostrophe is ignored
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: To shine, someone will escort a girl called Havergal to church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Havergal' looks like a girl's name; Havergal Brian was an English composer, and 'take ... round' wraps his surname around I'LL.
explanation.definitionFit: Brilliance is dazzling brightness or magnificence.

clue.text: Perfect place for opera within limits

explanation.walkthrough: 'within limits' points to the opera's full title, Utopia, Limited.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopia is an ideal land, and Utopia, Limited is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera.

clue.text: A defector, a senior rating, say

parts.note: a petty officer, PO, is a senior rating in the Royal Navy
to state is to say

explanation.surface: A naval petty officer is described as having changed sides.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Royal Navy a 'rating' is a sailor who is not an officer; 'say' is a verb here, not a homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostate is someone who abandons their faith or party.

clue.text: Story that's 29

explanation.walkthrough: 29 is GREEK, from 29 across. 'Story' is the floor of a house, not a tale.
explanation.definitionFit: An attic is a top floor (an old spelling of storey), and Attic was the dialect of ancient Athens, a form of Greek.

clue.text: Coming out second, worsted in a reversal

indicators.note: in a reversal says the joined letters are read backwards

parts.note: serge is a hard-wearing worsted cloth

explanation.surface: Someone emerges second, beaten after a turn of fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worsted' looks like 'beaten', but it is the wool cloth: 'in a reversal' turns S and SERGE backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Egress is the act of going out, or a way out.

clue.text: Times editorial starts off "Exterminate"

parts.note: eras are times or periods

indicators.note: starts off means just the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A Times newspaper editorial begins with a call to destroy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper, but it is ERAS.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to wipe out completely, so to destroy.

clue.text: Flower is double

indicators.note: double says the word is written twice

explanation.surface: A bloom is twice the size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is a river, something that flows: the Isis is the name of the Thames at Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isis is the stretch of the River Thames through Oxford.

clue.text: Some boy scouts are too French about love

indicators.note: about says the French word goes around the letter for love

parts.note: trop is French for too
love is zero in tennis, a round O

explanation.surface: Scouts are said to be overly French in their love of things.
explanation.definitionFit: A troop is a unit of scouts led together.

clue.text: Caning scholars can lead to trouble

parts.note: BAs are graduates, Bachelors of Arts
a tin is a can
ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: School pupils who get caned face trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a verb, but it is the noun TIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The bastinado is a punishment of beating the soles of the feet with a stick.

clue.text: In musical instruments, tastes can vary

indicators.note: vary tells us the letters of these two words change their order

explanation.surface: People's taste in instruments differs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vary' tells you to rearrange TASTES and CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Castanets are Spanish clicking hand-held percussion shells.

clue.text: In some degree, know a foreign language

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: To some extent, a person knows another tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' says the answer is in plain sight: the letters spanning 'deGREE, Know'.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek is the language of Greece, foreign to a British solver.
